analysis.one_liner: Requires fuel sellers to cut the carbon pollution of transportation fuels while roughly doubling mandated renewable fuel volumes.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Sen. Barack Obama in May 2007, the bill was sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required oil refiners and fuel importers to reduce the average lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions of the fuel they sell — about 5% below 2007 levels by 2015 and 10% by 2020 — by blending in low-carbon fuels such as ethanol and cellulosic biofuels, with a credit-trading system for companies that cut more than required. It also would have roughly doubled the government-mandated volumes of renewable fuel through 2012, from about 7.5 billion gallons to 15 billion, and required growing volumes of ultra-low-carbon fuels through 2025 and beyond. The bill combined real climate policy with a large guaranteed market for the biofuels industry.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people would benefit from reduced transportation emissions, less dependence on imported oil, and preserved state authority to adopt stricter rules. The biofuels industry — ethanol producers, cellulosic fuel developers, and the farmers who supply feedstock — would gain a federally guaranteed and expanding market for their product, with credits worth 2.5 conventional gallons for each gallon of cellulosic ethanol.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and climate; biofuel and farm interests

how_it_helps.text: Requires each obligated party — refiners and fuel importers — to reduce the average lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions of the fuel they sell to at least 5% below the 2005–2007 baseline by 2015 and at least 10% below by 2020, with further reductions of 2% every five years after 2025 [S3].
Establishes a certification and labeling process so consumers can identify and choose low-carbon fuels at the pump [S3].
Preserves state authority: if a state law requires equal or greater greenhouse gas reductions, the stricter state law applies instead of the federal standard [S3].

Doubles the required renewable fuel volumes to 12–15 billion gallons for 2009–2012 and mandates growing volumes of ultra-low-carbon fuels (at least 50% or 75% below conventional fuel's emissions) reaching 21 billion gallons combined by 2025, with no per-gallon cap and credits for exceeding requirements [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil refiners and fuel importers bear the cost of blending low-carbon fuels and buying credits; those costs are generally passed through to consumers in fuel prices. Consumers at the pump and taxpayers indirectly bear costs if expanded biofuel production raises crop and food prices or drives land conversion — risks the bill itself acknowledges by requiring a sustainability study of deforestation, land use, water quality, and wildlife impacts.
analysis.who_pays_short: Refiners, and consumers at the pump

drawbacks.text: The bill itself directs the EPA to study whether increased biofuel volumes cause deforestation, land-use change, and harm to water and air quality, acknowledging that not all renewable fuel is environmentally benign [S3].

Doubling the renewable fuel mandate from 7.5 to 15 billion gallons in four years benefits corn ethanol producers regardless of actual carbon performance, and compliance costs on refiners tend to be passed to consumers at the pump.

The bill includes waiver provisions letting the EPA reduce or suspend the ultra-low-carbon requirements if implementation would severely harm the economy or if domestic supply is inadequate, giving industry a defined exit from the mandate [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core low-carbon fuel standard is a genuine, enforceable climate policy with consumer benefits and preserved state authority. But the bill bundles it with a large, blanket expansion of renewable fuel volumes that serves the established biofuel and farm interests alongside the environmental goal, and it leaves fuel-price effects on consumers unaddressed. A well-designed version would tie all subsidies and mandates to measured carbon performance rather than volume.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in May 2007, and no committee action, floor vote, or companion movement ever followed before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Barack Obama introduced the National Low-Carbon Fuel Standard Act of 2007 on May 7, 2007, with introductory remarks in the Senate [S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day [S5].
The action history shows no further activity — no hearings, markup, committee vote, or floor action — between the referral and the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009 [S5].
The bill attracted two Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support during its lifetime [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil refiners and fuel importers avoided a new compliance obligation on the carbon content of their fuels. The established biofuel industry also lost nothing, since the broader renewable fuel mandate it favored was enacted later that year in separate legislation; the public got neither the emissions cuts nor the pump costs this bill would have produced.

for.name: Sen. Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor on May 7, 2007.

for.name: Senate Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no Republican cosponsored.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; Chair was Sen. Barbara Boxer (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists; its sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have doubled mandated renewable fuel volumes and created rising ultra-low-carbon fuel requirements through 2025, making biofuel producers the permanent channel for a public emissions-reduction goal. Cellulosic ethanol would have earned credits worth 2.5 conventional gallons per gallon. In return the bill imposes carbon-intensity and environmental sustainability standards on those fuels.
A doubled renewable fuel mandate means a larger guaranteed market for feedstock crops. Consumers could pay indirectly through higher crop and food prices.

They would become obligated parties required to cut the carbon intensity of every gallon sold or buy credits, with compliance costs generally passed to consumers at the pump. The bill's waiver provisions gave them a defined escape hatch.

industries.industry: Electric vehicle and hydrogen fuel industries
industries.note: The bill requires the EPA to credit electricity and hydrogen fuels with their per-mile greenhouse gas advantage when counting compliance, giving those fuels a favorable position in the standard.
